title: The Tonic Chaleo Yoovidhya Sold to Thailand's Truck Drivers
dek: In 1976 a Bangkok pharmaceutical seller launched Krating Daeng, a cheap, better-tasting tonic aimed at labourers and drivers rather than the capital's richer buyers.

story.event: Launching the Krating Daeng tonic for Thai labourers and truck drivers
story.summary: Chaleo Yoovidhya, born poor in Phichit province, sold antibiotics in Bangkok and founded TC Pharmaceutical (1956 by the company's account, 1962 in obituaries). In 1976 he introduced Krating Daeng, a cheap, better-tasting, uncarbonated tonic aimed at truck drivers, labourers and shift workers rather than Bangkok's wealthier buyers; within a year it was Thailand's second-best-selling tonic. In 1984 he and Dietrich Mateschitz founded Red Bull GmbH.
paragraphs: In 1976 a new tonic went on sale in Thailand. Krating Daeng, Thai for red gaur, was a syrupy, uncarbonated tonic sold through pharmacies, and its makers did not aim it at Bangkok's comfortable buyers. They aimed it at people who worked long, hard hours.

Its maker was Chaleo Yoovidhya. He had been born in Phichit province, in northern Thailand, to poor Chinese immigrant parents; obituaries disagree on the year, giving 1923 or 1932. He had worked as a bus conductor, a fruit seller and on the family's duck farm before moving to Bangkok to help his brother run a chemist's shop and becoming a salesman of antibiotics. He then set up his own firm, TC Pharmaceutical. The company dates it to 1956, as a partnership importing medicines from Europe; obituaries say 1962.

After about twenty years in medicines, the company's history says, he saw that energy tonics had room to grow in Thailand, but the ones on sale tasted like medicine, so he worked on one that tasted better. The formula combined caffeine with taurine, an amino acid, and glucuronolactone, a carbohydrate. He kept the price low and positioned it for labourers rather than city buyers, with heavy advertising and giveaways to truck drivers, construction workers and shift workers. It was sold as a stimulant for day labourers, long-haul truckers and rickshaw drivers. Within a year of launch, The Independent later reported, it was second only to Japan's Lipovitan-D.

In 1982 an Austrian toothpaste salesman, Dietrich Mateschitz, found that the drink eased his jet lag. In 1984 he proposed a partnership, and he and Chaleo each put in $500,000 to found Red Bull GmbH, with 49 per cent each and the remaining 2 per cent for Chaleo's son Chalerm. Carbonating it was Mateschitz's idea, and Red Bull went on sale in Austria in 1987. Chaleo gave no interviews for the last 30 years of his life. He died in Bangkok in March 2012.

quote.text: That the true piety which most removes Earth-aches and ills, where one is moderate In eating and in resting, and in sport; Measured in wish and act; sleeping betimes, Waking betimes for duty.
quote.locator: Chapter VI, "Atmasanyamayog, or The Book of Religion by Self-Restraint" (verses 16-17 in the usual numbering)
quote.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gîtâ, tr. Sir Edwin Arnold, Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
quote.connection: Chaleo's tonic sold wakefulness to people who had to keep working when tired. The Gita praises a life measured in rest, sleeping betimes and waking betimes for duty. Both take the labourer's day seriously; they disagree about what to do with the tiredness.

reflection: Chaleo made something for people whose work did not stop when they were tired: long-haul drivers, labourers, shift workers. He priced it for them and sold it where they were, and it worked because he understood who was buying.

The Gita's line sits awkwardly beside that, and it should. Some days a lift to keep going is the right help. On other days the honest answer to tiredness is sleep, and no formula changes that. You will know which kind of day this is better from your own body than from any advertisement.
invitation: Tonight, notice the hour at which you would usually reach for something to keep you going. Go to bed at that hour instead, just once, and see what tomorrow morning makes of it.

sources.title: Chaleo Yoovidhya: Recluse who created the Red Bull energy drink (Martin Childs, 21 March 2012)
sources.supports: Born to a poor Chinese-Thai family in Phichit in 1923; duck farming and fruit trading; helped his brother run a chemist shop in Bangkok and sold antibiotics; set up TC Pharmaceuticals in the 1960s; formula of caffeine, taurine and glucuronolactone after years of work; introduced in 1976 and second only to Lipovitan-D within a year; ignored Bangkok and positioned the drink for labourers with low prices, heavy advertising and giveaways to truck drivers, construction workers and shift workers; Mateschitz's 1982 discovery, 1984 proposal to carbonate and launch globally; $500,000 each, 49 per cent each and the rest to Chaleo's son Chalerm; Red Bull sold in Austria from 1987; died in Bangkok on 17 March 2012.

sources.title: Red bull's co-founder dies in Bangkok (Associated Press, 20 March 2012)
sources.supports: Born to poor Chinese immigrants in Phichit; bus conductor, fruit vendor and duck farmer; founded T.C. Pharmaceuticals, a maker of antibiotics and cosmetics, in 1962; Krating Daeng a syrupy energy tonic sold in pharmacies as a stimulant for day labourers, long-haul truckers and rickshaw drivers; Mateschitz's 1982 trip; carbonation was Mateschitz's idea; Red Bull released in 1987.

sources.title: Red Bull creator and Thai tycoon Chaleo Yoovidhya dead (17 March 2012)
sources.supports: Born to poor Chinese immigrant parents in Phichit, reportedly in 1932; salesman before setting up TC Pharmaceuticals in 1962; Krating Daeng popular with shift workers and lorry drivers; launched as Red Bull with Mateschitz in 1984 and sold in Austria three years later.

sources.title: Chaleo Yoovidhya, 1923-2012: The duck farmer's son who created Red Bull (2012)
sources.supports: Family raised ducks and sold fruit; by the early 1960s he had saved enough to found a small pharmaceutical firm; invented Krating Daeng in 1976 and marketed it to blue-collar workers and truck drivers; $500,000 each from Chaleo and Mateschitz; gave no interviews for the last 30 years of his life.

sources.title: Krating Daeng
sources.supports: Supplementary only: the name Krating Daeng refers to the gaur; introduced in Thailand in 1976 for rural labourers.

cross_checks.claim: Chaleo was born in Phichit province to poor Chinese immigrant parents and sold antibiotics before founding TC Pharmaceutical.
TC Pharmaceutical was founded in 1956 (company account) or 1962 (obituaries).
The tonic was aimed at labourers, truck drivers and shift workers rather than wealthier city buyers.
In 1984 Chaleo and Mateschitz founded Red Bull GmbH, and Red Bull went on sale in Austria in 1987.

research_notes: No founder voice: The Week notes Chaleo gave no interviews for the last 30 years of his life, so the story attributes no thoughts or words to him; his reasoning about taste and growth is the company's own 2011 account, attributed as such. Birth year: The Independent and The Week give 1923, the BBC 'reportedly 1932' from local media; obituaries put his age at death between 88 and 90; the story gives both years. Company founding: the company profile says 1956, as a limited partnership importing European medicines; AP and the BBC say 1962; The Independent 'the 1960s'; The Week 'the early 1960s'. The story gives the company's date and the obituaries' date. Launch year: The Independent, The Week and Wikipedia say 1976 (Wikipedia also says first devised in 1975), the BBC only 'the 1970s'; the company profile says T.C. Pharmaceutical Industries was formed in 1978 to research and develop the product and 'later launched' it, which could be read as a later date. The story uses 1976, the date the independent obituaries agree on, and does not claim the 1978 company launched it. The Lipovitan-D ranking rests on The Independent alone and is attributed to it. 'Toothpaste salesman' follows The Independent, AP and The Week; other accounts describe Mateschitz's employer differently. Wikipedia is used once, as a supplementary source for the gaur name. Funding is set to bootstrapped because the drink was developed inside Chaleo's own firm, which The Week says he founded from savings; no outside investment before Red Bull GmbH is reported. The tonic later became the basis of Red Bull, which is mentioned only as the aftermath; the episode is the 1976 Thai launch. Quote: Arnold's Chapter VI corresponds to verses 6.16-17 in the usual numbering; the excerpt begins after 'call', mid-sentence.
